Cancer under the microscope

Pancreatic cancer.
One organ, distinct cell systems.

The pancreas contains exocrine cells that support digestion and endocrine cells that produce hormones. Cancers from these systems are not the same disease.

IN THIS GUIDETwo cell systemsThe common formTissue vs. cytologyWhat classification addsSources

“Pancreatic cancer” can describe tumors with different cells of origin and different behavior. The microscopic diagnosis establishes which disease is actually present.

01 / CELL OF ORIGIN

Exocrine and endocrine cells do different jobs.

Most of the pancreas is made of exocrine tissue, which produces enzymes involved in digestion. Smaller groups of endocrine cells make hormones. Tumors arising from these systems are classified separately because their biology and treatment differ.

EXOCRINE

Ductal and related cancers

Exocrine cancers are much more common. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is the best-known type.

ENDOCRINE

Neuroendocrine tumors

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors begin in hormone-producing cells and form a distinct group.

02 / DUCTAL ADENOCARCINOMA

The most common form is not the only form.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is an exocrine cancer. On a tissue section, pathologists assess gland formation, cell features, invasion, and the surrounding response. A small cropped image can introduce the pattern, but classification requires multiple fields and the full specimen.

03 / SPECIMEN CONTEXT

Tissue sections and cytology answer with different context.

A tissue section preserves architecture: the relationship between tumor, ducts, supporting tissue, vessels, and other structures. Cytology emphasizes individual cells or small groups collected by a needle, brush, or fluid. Both can be useful, but they do not look identical and should never be treated as interchangeable images.

READ THE LABEL

The image on the right is a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm—not pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Similar location does not mean identical disease.

04 / BEYOND THE IMAGE

Type, grade, stage, and testing complete the record.

Microscopy identifies a tumor’s pattern and cell lineage. Grade describes differentiation and appearance; stage describes extent. Imaging, laboratory results, and sometimes molecular tests provide evidence that a microscope image alone cannot.
